references.text: Moses stretches out his hand toward the sky to bring hail upon Egypt, the same action used here to bring darkness.
The psalm describes how God sent darkness and made it dark in Egypt, a direct reference to this plague.
Isaiah describes darkness and distress over the land, using similar language about darkness as God's judgment.
Joel describes the day of the Lord as a day of darkness and gloom, with the same theme of darkness as a sign of God's judgment.
Amos describes the day of the Lord as darkness and not light, using darkness as an image of God's judgment.
The same command to Moses to stretch out his hand to perform a miracle, here with the staff over the waters of Egypt.
The fifth angel pours out his bowl on the throne of the beast, and its kingdom is plunged into darkness - parallel to the plague of darkness over Egypt.
Darkness came over the whole land when Jesus hung on the cross, similar supernatural darkness as a sign of God's action.
Darkness was over the deep at creation, and God separated light from darkness - a foundational text about darkness and light.
The same prophetic gesture toward the sky leads to different forms of judgment (hail and darkness), emphasizing God's sovereign control over nature.
Connects plagues where the hand is stretched out to bring destruction upon the earth's fertility (locusts) and then total darkness.
The same gesture ('stretch out your hand') is first used to bring death upon Egypt (the plagues) and later to save Israel at the Red Sea.
Describes the actual execution of a sky-directed plague (hail) as parallel to the command for the plague of darkness.
Contrasts 'thick darkness' as judgment over Egypt with 'thick cloud' as a sign of God's presence and revelation to Israel.
